title: What Is Companion Care and How Is It Different Than Medical Home Care?
summary: Learn what companion care for seniors is, what services it includes, how it differs from medical home care, and how it can support independence.
body_markdown:
Maintaining your independence in your golden years doesn’t mean you have to do everything by yourself. “Independence” means having the freedom to make your own choices and continue enjoying the people, places, and activities that make life meaningful to you.


Sometimes, a little extra support can make all that easier. You may not need a nurse or hands-on medical care, but you might benefit from having someone join you for coffee, accompany you to the zoo, help with errands, or spend time with you at home. That’s where companion care can help.


**Companion care is a type of non-medical support that provides conversation, social connection, everyday assistance, and company at home or in the community.** Unlike medical home care, it doesn’t involve skilled nursing, medical treatments, or clinical services. Companion care can make your days feel a little easier, safer, and more enjoyable while helping you remain active, connected, and in control of your life.


In this guide, we’ll explain how companion care works, what a care companion may help you with, and how it differs from medical home care.


## **What Is Companion Care for Seniors?**


Companion care for seniors focuses on improving the social and practical parts of daily life. A companion might visit you at home, join you for an outing, help you stay engaged in your favorite activities, or provide a reassuring and consistent presence while family members are unavailable.


Companion care services are non-medical. The companion is there to provide company, encouragement, and practical support, ***not*** to diagnose health conditions, administer medical treatments, or replace a doctor or nurse.


Depending on your needs, companion care may include:


- Conversation and social interaction
- Playing cards, completing puzzles, or working on hobbies
- [Going for a walk with you](https://www.gogograndparent.com/blog/how-to-add-walking-into-your-daily-routine-for-national-walking-day)
- Accompanying you to lunch, coffee, or a community activity
- Helping with errands or shopping
- Preparing a simple meal
- Offering[medication reminders](https://gogograndparent.com/blog/medication-adherence-for-seniors)
- Helping organize mail, appointments, or a weekly schedule
- Providing light household support
- Checking in on your general well-being
- Giving family caregivers a break


## **Companion Care Can Help You Stay Independent**


You may be perfectly capable of completing many daily tasks on your own. But that doesn’t mean every task *has* to be handled alone. Having a companion can give you extra confidence and make everyday life feel more enjoyable, connected, and satisfying.


Maybe you still enjoy grocery shopping, but you’d feel more comfortable having someone walk through the store with you. Maybe you miss going to museums, local events, or your favorite coffee shop but don’t enjoy attending by yourself. Or perhaps the house simply feels too quiet during certain parts of the week.


Companion care may be especially helpful for you if:


- Your family or friends live far away.
- Friends are no longer able to visit as often.
- You have[stopped driving](https://gogograndparent.com/blog/alternatives-to-driving-for-seniors) or prefer not to drive in certain conditions.
- You feel uneasy going to unfamiliar places alone.
- You recently lost a spouse, partner, or close friend.
- You’re recovering from an illness but don’t require medical home care.
- You’d like to become more[socially active](https://www.gogograndparent.com/blog/feeling-disconnected-try-these-11-ways-to-rebuild-your-social-circle-this-season) and want someone to help you through that.
- You want someone to check in regularly.
- You’d enjoy having social time to look forward to during the week.


Keep in mind that accepting help does not mean losing your independence. In many cases, the right support can help you protect your independence for even longer.


## **What Does In-Home Companion Care for Seniors Include?**


Although it’s often called in-home companion care, the support doesn’t necessarily have to be provided inside your home. A companion may visit you at home, but they can often also accompany you around the community (depending on the provider and services available).


### ***Companionship at Home***


Your home is where you should feel most comfortable, but even familiar routines can feel more enjoyable when they’re shared. At home, a companion might:


- Sit and talk with you over coffee or tea
- Watch your favorite movie or television show with you
- Help you organize family photographs
- Help you declutter your closet or cabinets
- Play cards or a board game
- Work on a craft or puzzle with you
- Read aloud
- Help you write letters or greeting cards
- Join you while you make a favorite recipe
- Take a walk with you around the neighborhood
- Help you make a video call to family or friends
- Sit with you while you wait for a delivery or home repair appointment


### ***Companionship Outside Your Home***


You may also want a companion to join you for activities outside the home. Having someone beside you can make the outing easier, more comfortable, and more fun. Depending on your interests, that could mean going together for:


- Coffee or lunch
- A trip to the zoo or aquarium
- A museum visit
- A walk through a park or botanical garden
- A movie or community performance
- A senior-center class or activity
- A library event
- Shopping
- A religious service
- A family gathering
- A doctor’s appointment
- A visit with an old friend


### **Companion Care vs. Medical Home Care**


The terms “companion care” and “medical home care” sound similar, but they serve very different purposes.


**Companion care is non-medical.** It focuses on social connection, everyday activities, light assistance, and having someone nearby.


**Medical home care is clinical.** It’s provided by qualified healthcare professionals and is used to treat, monitor, or manage a medical condition.


You may benefit from **companion care** if you’d like:


- More conversation and social interaction
- Someone to join you for activities or outings
- Encouragement to stay active and involved
- Light help with errands or routines
- A reassuring presence at home
- Support getting out into your community


You may need **medical home care** if you require:


- Skilled nursing
- Wound care
- Injections or other clinical treatments
- Physical, occupational, or speech therapy
- Medical monitoring
- Care prescribed after an illness, surgery, injury, or hospitalization


**The two services do not have to be mutually exclusive.** You may receive medical home health visits for a specific condition *and* have a companion visit for conversation, errands, or social activities.


## **How Does Companion Care Work?**


Companion care can be arranged around your needs, preferences, and schedule. You might enjoy having someone visit for a few hours once a week, several shorter visits throughout the week, or during particular outings and activities. For example, you might arrange for someone to:


- Visit every Tuesday afternoon for conversation and a walk
- Go grocery shopping with you once a week
- Join you for a monthly museum or zoo trip
- Have lunch with you weekly while a family caregiver is busy
- Accompany you to community events
- Check in after you return home from the hospital
- Spend time with you while relatives are out of town
- Help you[continue a beloved hobby](https://www.gogograndparent.com/blog/how-to-find-senior-hobbies-in-the-golden-years) or pursue a new one


Start by thinking about the moments you could use more company or support. Are there places you’ve stopped going because you don’t want to go alone? Are certain days of the week especially quiet? Are there errands or activities you keep postponing? Your answers can help you decide what kind of companion care would make the biggest difference in your life.


The exact responsibilities can vary between providers, so it’s important to ask what’s included before arranging care. You want to be clear on what kind of help you’ll receive and make sure you[feel comfortable with the person entering your home](https://www.gogograndparent.com/blog/how-to-feel-comfortable-with-a-new-caregiver-at-home) .


## **Other Care Options You May Want to Consider**


Your needs may also change over time. What works for you today may look different several months or years from now, and that is perfectly normal. Companion care is only one of several types of support available to help you stay comfortable and independent in your home. Some other care options you might consider include:


### ***Personal Care***


Personal care offers more hands-on assistance with daily activities, such as bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, eating, or moving around safely. This may be helpful if you feel steady and independent in some areas but need physical aid with others due to arthritis, injury, or chronic conditions.


### ***Homemaker Services***


Homemaker services focus on tasks around the home, such as:


- Light cleaning
- Laundry
- Meal preparation
- Grocery shopping
- Changing bed linens
- Organizing household items


Keeping up with a home takes a great deal of time and energy. Getting help with these tasks can allow you to save that energy for the people and activities you enjoy.

### ***Medical Home Health Care***


[Medical home health care](https://gogograndparent.com/blog/home-care-vs-assisted-living) provides skilled services by nurses, therapists, or other licensed healthcare professionals. It often includes nursing care, therapy, wound care, or medical monitoring. You may need this type of care after an illness, injury, surgery, or hospital stay.


### ***Adult Day Programs***


Adult day programs give you a place to enjoy activities, meals, exercise, entertainment, and social time with others your age. They may be a good option if you want more structure and regular opportunities to meet other people.


### ***Transportation Services***


Giving up driving can feel like giving up part of your freedom, but transportation services can keep you moving where you want and need to go. You may use them for:


- Medical appointments
- Shopping
- Lunch with friends
- Religious services
- Classes and community activities

## **Will Medicare Pay for Companion Care?**


Medicare generally does not cover companion care when companionship or non-medical support is the only service you need. It may cover certain skilled home health services when you meet specific medical and eligibility requirements, but social visits, general supervision, homemaker services, and non-medical companionship are not usually covered on their own.


Your options may be different if you have:


- Medicaid
- A Medicare Advantage plan
- Long-term care insurance
- Veterans benefits
- State or local aging programs
- Other private benefits


Before arranging services, contact your insurance plan or benefits provider. Ask which types of care are covered, which providers you can use, and whether you need approval before services begin. A trusted family member or insurance representative may be able to help you understand your choices.


## **How to Choose a Companion Care Service**


Inviting someone into your home is personal. You deserve a companion who treats you with kindness, listens to you, and respects your preferences. Before selecting a companion care service or agency, consider asking the following questions:


- Are companions screened and background-checked?
- What kind of training do they receive?
- Can I meet the companion before services begin?
- Will the same person visit me regularly?
- What activities can the companion help with?
- Can the companion join me for activities outside my home?
- Is transportation available or included?
- What happens if my regular companion is unavailable?
- Is there a minimum number of hours per visit?
- How are schedule changes handled?
- Who should I contact if I have a concern?
- How much does the service cost?


Pay attention to how you feel during your first conversations with the provider and companion. Do they speak directly to you rather than only addressing your family members? Do they ask about your preferences? Do you feel listened to and respected? The right companion will make you feel *more* comfortable, not less, in your daily life.
